title: Red Meat Safety, Quality and Good Manufacturing Practices (GMPs)

lessons.title: Meat safety hazards in sheep and goat slaughter
lessons.html:
Safe mutton, lamb and chevon

Lamb, mutton and goat meat (chevon) from your abattoir will be eaten at braais, family meals and ceremonies. If it carries harmful germs, chemicals or objects, people can get sick. Many hazards cannot be seen, so you must follow the rules all the time.

Three kinds of hazards

HazardExamples in small stock slaughter
BiologicalGerms such as E. coli and Salmonella from the wool, hair, dung and gut; parasites such as tapeworm cysts
ChemicalMedicine or dip residues if animals are slaughtered before the withdrawal period on the product label has passed; cleaning chemicals
PhysicalWool, hair, knife tips, plastic, jewellery, bone splinters

The wool and skin are the biggest risk

Sheep wool and goat hair carry a lot of dirt and dung. During skinning, the outside of the skin must never touch the meat. Even one touch transfers germs. Wool on the carcass must be trimmed off. Your hands and knife must be cleaned after touching the outside of the skin and before touching the meat.

Quality

Customers want carcasses that are clean, with no wool, hair, bruises or blood clots, well chilled and correctly classified. Good quality depends on:

  • Calm handling before slaughter, to avoid bruises and stress.
  • Careful skinning, so the fat cover is not torn and the meat is not cut.
  • Clean evisceration with no gut spills.
  • Fast chilling.

lessons.title: Good Manufacturing Practices for people
lessons.html:
What GMPs are

Good Manufacturing Practices (GMPs) are the basic rules that keep food safe. In an abattoir they cover people, equipment, the building, cleaning, water, pests and waste. The first and most important part is you.

Personal hygiene

  • Wear clean protective clothing every day: overall, apron, hairnet, white boots. Change in the change room.
  • Wash hands and arms with soap and warm water before work, after the toilet, after breaks, and whenever they are dirty. Rub for at least 20 seconds.
  • Remove jewellery and watches. Keep nails short and clean.
  • Do not eat, drink, smoke, chew gum or spit in work areas.
  • Cover cuts with a blue waterproof plaster and a glove.
  • Report illness, such as diarrhoea, vomiting, fever or infected sores, before your shift.
  • Do not wear protective clothing outside the work area.

Knife hygiene

  • Use two knives where your plant allows it: one in use, one in the sterilizer.
  • Sterilise the knife after each carcass and after touching the skin, wool or anything dirty.
  • Never put a knife down on the floor, or hold it in your mouth or under your arm.

The two-hand rule in skinning

Many abattoirs teach a rule: one hand touches only the outside of the skin, and the other hand touches only the meat side. This lowers the chance of carrying dirt from the wool onto the carcass. Follow the method your trainer shows you.

lessons.title: GMPs for the line and the building
lessons.html:
Preventing cross-contamination

  • Keep the dirty area (skinning) and clean area (evisceration) separate.
  • Carcasses must not touch each other, the floor, walls, platforms or drains.
  • If a carcass falls on the floor, report it and follow the plant procedure.
  • Keep edible and inedible products in separate, marked containers.
  • Keep heads, feet and skins away from carcasses.

Cleaning and water

  • Clean and sanitise equipment and surfaces according to the cleaning schedule.
  • Only clean, potable water may touch meat.
  • Keep drains clear and floors free of wool and fat.

Pests

Flies, rats, birds and cats carry germs. Keep doors closed, keep waste covered, and report any pest you see.

Temperature control

Germs grow fast on warm meat. Carcasses must go to the chiller promptly and stay cold until dispatch. Check and record chiller temperatures as your plant procedure says, and report problems.

HACCP

Many abattoirs use HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points). The plant identifies the steps where hazards must be controlled, such as zero visible contamination on carcasses and chiller temperature. Workers at those steps check, record, and tell the supervisor at once if something goes wrong.

Key points

  • Hazards can be biological, chemical or physical, and most cannot be seen.
  • The outside of the skin and the wool must never touch the meat.
  • Wash hands often, wear clean protective clothing and no jewellery.
  • Sterilise knives after each carcass and after touching the skin.
  • Keep carcasses off the floor and away from each other.
  • Chill carcasses quickly and record temperatures honestly.
